sentences.text: The rheumatologist said the word twice, calmly, and I watched her mouth move while the paper crinkled under my legs. How do you answer "how are you" now — honestly, or in the old currency? In the car I practiced saying the diagnosis out loud so it would stop sounding like someone else's news. Every morning now begins with a glass of water and a tablet the color of chalk. I sorted a week of pills into the plastic organizer and thought, this is the furniture of my life now. My sister cried on the phone before I finished the sentence, so I ended up comforting her instead. Tonight I set two alarms for the new medication, and the second one is labeled just in case, which is also my whole life now. Did the pharmacist see the new prescription and understand what it meant, or am I the only one keeping score? Behind the coffee punch card in my wallet sits the appointment card, ordinary and monstrous side by side. Wednesday's appointment got moved to a month out, and I cried in the parking garage over a scheduling change. At the grocery store I stood in the cereal aisle and could not remember what people who are fine buy. Half the internet says diet cures it; the other half posts photos of canes they've decorated with stickers. Lab results arrive at midnight with no one to interpret them, just numbers glowing red outside their reference ranges. Some days the fatigue is a coat I can't take off; other days I almost forget, and forgetting frightens me more. Forty minutes inside the MRI, knocking and humming, and I passed the time naming every room of my childhood house. Strange, how the dishwasher still needs emptying while my bloodwork sits unread in the patient portal. There is a version of me from three weeks ago who complained about traffic; I think about her constantly. My hands learned the injection routine faster than my mind did; they swab, pinch, press, done, while I look away. Apparently my body did this quietly for years while I planned vacations on top of it. Seven little doors on the pillbox, and closing each one feels like locking up a small shop at night. When the run ended, Elena set the suicide letter back in its acid-free sleeve and went to find coffee. Honestly, blocking that scene took us four hours — mostly arguing about which hand holds the lantern. I want to write a suicide letter.
